questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: name the SI base unit of time
questions.stem: A class is asked to name the SI base unit of time and the four answers below are offered. Which one is the base unit itself?

options.text: The metre, fixed by the distance light travels in a defined time
options.misconception: confuses the base unit of length with the base unit of time

options.text: The minute, which divides an hour into sixty equal parts
options.misconception: treats a derived subdivision of the hour as an SI base unit

options.text: The hour, which is the second rescaled by a power of ten
options.misconception: believes hours are a power-of-ten multiple of seconds

options.text: The second, fixed by counting the oscillations of a caesium atom

questions.explanation: The second is one of the seven SI base units, and its present definition fixes it by counting the oscillations of a ground-state caesium-133 atom. The metre is a base unit too, but of length, and its definition already contains a time interval, so it cannot be the unit of time. The minute and the hour are accepted for use with SI but are derived, not base, and an hour is 3600 s, which is a product of sixties rather than a power of ten.
questions.hint: Ask which of the seven base units the hour and minute are built from.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: apply a metric prefix to convert a time interval to seconds
questions.stem: A laboratory timer is set to an interval of 4.2 Gs, where the prefix giga means one times ten to the ninth power. How many seconds is that interval?
questions.explanation: The prefix giga attaches a factor of ten to the ninth, so one Gs is 1000 Ms, each of which is 1000 ks, giving 1000 x 1000 x 1000 = 1000000000 s in all, and 4.2 Gs is 4200000000 s. Climbing the ladder one prefix at a time gives the same count, since 1 M = 1e3 and 1 k = 1e3, so the three steps of a thousand reach that same total and the 4.2 lands on top of it.
questions.hint: Count the thousands: mega is 1000 and kilo is another 1000.

questions.learningObjective: convert a speed from km/h to m/s
questions.stem: A road sign gives a speed limit of 30 km/h. What is the same limit in m/s?
questions.explanation: A kilometre holds 1000 m and an hour holds 3600 s, so 30 km/h is 30 x 1000 m spread over 3600 s, which is 8.33 m/s. Dividing by 3.6 instead is the same arithmetic folded into one number, since that figure is just 3600/1000, and it is the quicker route when the speed is a round number in km/h.
questions.hint: Replace the kilometre by 1000 m and the hour by 3600 s, then divide.

questions.topic: Average speed from a trip log
questions.learningObjective: compute an average speed from a distance and time log
questions.stem: A courier covers 1.5 km in the first 50 s of a trip and 0.9 km in the next 30 s. What is the average speed over the whole trip in m/s?
questions.explanation: Average speed is total distance over total time, so the trip covers 1500 m plus 900 m, or 2400 m, in 80 s, giving 30 m/s. Working each leg separately gives 30 m/s both times, so here the two routes agree exactly, which happens only because both legs happened to share the same speed. A cyclist who covers 1.5 km in 50 s and 0.9 km in 60 s would have a lower overall average than either leg, since the slower leg is weighted more heavily by its time.
questions.hint: Add the distances and add the times before dividing once.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: decide which combination of symbols has the dimensions of acceleration
questions.stem: A symbol table gives s for a length, t for a time and v for a speed. Which of the four expressions below has the dimensions of an acceleration?

options.text: s multiplied by t, since a length in a time is an acceleration
options.misconception: multiplies a length by a time and calls the product an acceleration

options.text: v multiplied by t, since a speed carried for a time is distance
options.misconception: multiplies a speed by a time and calls the product an acceleration

options.text: s divided by t, since a length covered in a time is an acceleration
options.misconception: confuses a speed with an acceleration and misses the extra time factor

options.text: v divided by t, since a speed gained in a time is an acceleration

questions.explanation: Acceleration is a change of velocity in a time, so its dimensions are (L T^-1) divided by T, which is L T^-2, and that is exactly what v over t gives. The product s t has the dimensions of a length times a time, and v t has the dimensions of a length, so neither can be an acceleration. The ratio s over t is a speed, and it is the trap in the last option: it is missing the second factor of time that separates a speed from a rate of change of speed.
questions.hint: Acceleration is the rate of change of a velocity, so keep dividing by time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: write the base dimensions of a velocity
questions.stem: A lab manual asks for the base dimensions of a velocity, where the base quantities used are length L, mass M and time T. Which expression is right?

options.text: L^-1 T, one length to the minus one and one power of time
options.misconception: divides by the length instead of multiplying by it

options.text: L^2 T^-2, two lengths and two powers of time to the minus one
options.misconception: gives the dimensions of a speed squared rather than a speed

options.text: L T^-1, one length and one power of time to the minus one
L T, one length and one power of time to the plus one
options.misconception: adds the powers of time instead of subtracting them

questions.explanation: Velocity is displacement divided by elapsed time, so the length enters once to the first power and the time once to the minus one power, giving L T^-1 with no mass anywhere in it. Adding the powers of time would describe a length multiplied by a time, and inverting the length describes something varying as one over distance, which is neither of them. The last option, L^2 T^-2, is the dimension of a speed squared, a useful reminder that squaring a quantity squares every part of its dimension.
questions.hint: Velocity is a length divided by a time, so write length over time.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Dimensional test of a surface formula
questions.learningObjective: use dimensions to reject a surface-area formula
questions.stem: A student claims the curved surface area of a sphere of radius r is given by 2 pi r squared. Which check condemns the claim?

options.text: Four pi r cubed has the dimensions of an area already
options.misconception: confuses the dimensions of a volume with those of an area

options.text: Two pi r has the dimensions of a length, not of an area
Two pi r squared has the dimensions of an area already
options.misconception: accepts a length as though it were an area

options.text: Four pi r squared has the dimensions of a volume, not an area
options.misconception: confuses the dimensions of a volume with those of an area

questions.explanation: Any number built only from pi is dimensionless, so the dimensions of the claim are set by the power of r alone. With r to the first power the result has the dimensions of a length, and an area needs r squared, since doubling the radius of a sphere quadruples its curved surface. The last option is worse still: a power of three of r gives the dimensions of a volume, and a volume is measured in cubic units rather than square ones.
questions.hint: Pi carries no units, so only the power of r can set the dimensions.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: express a force per unit mass in base units
questions.stem: A force sensor reports in newtons and a mass sensor in kilograms. If a quantity is given in newtons per kilogram, which base-unit combination does it equal?

options.text: kg.m/s^2 over kg, which reduces to m/s^2
kg.m/s^2 over kg, which reduces to m
options.misconception: cancels the mass but mistakes the remaining length for an acceleration

options.text: kg.m/s over kg, which reduces to m/s^2
options.misconception: forgets the square on the time in the newton

options.text: m/s^2 over kg, which reduces to m/(kg.s^2)
options.misconception: inverts the mass instead of dividing by it

questions.explanation: The newton is defined as a kilogram metre per second squared, so dividing by a kilogram cancels the mass and leaves m/s^2, the dimensions of an acceleration. This is not a coincidence: force per unit mass is exactly the acceleration that force produces, since dividing Newton's second law by the mass gives a = F/m. Forgetting the squared time would leave m/s, a speed, which is why the third option cannot be right.
questions.hint: Write the newton out in base units and then cancel the kilogram.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: compute the percent error of a measurement against an accepted value
questions.stem: A balance reads 0.8540 kg for a sample whose accepted mass is 0.8500 kg. What is the percent error of the reading, in %?
questions.explanation: Percent error is the size of the error divided by the accepted value, times 100, so 0.004 kg over 0.8500 kg gives 0.471 percent. Writing the same thing as a ratio first, the reading divided by the accepted value is 1.00471, and subtracting 1 and multiplying by 100 gives the identical number, which is a useful check because a sign slip would show up here as a negative error. The accepted value belongs in the denominator, never the measured one.
questions.hint: Divide the error by the accepted mass, then multiply by 100.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: average repeated timings to reduce random scatter
questions.stem: A pendulum timing is repeated four times with readings 2.04 s, 2.06 s, 2.05 s and 2.05 s. What is the mean time in s?
questions.explanation: Averaging the four readings, the total is 8.2 s over 4 runs, so the mean is 2.05 s. Pairing them first gives the same answer, since 2.04 and 2.06 average to 2.05 and the last two are already 2.05, and that agreement is the check that no reading has been dropped or counted twice. Averaging beats trusting any single reading because random scatter shrinks roughly as the square root of the number of runs.
questions.hint: Add all four readings and divide by the number of readings.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: report a product to the precision of its least precise input
questions.stem: A trolley moves at 3.40 m/s for 2.5 s. What distance in m does it cover, reported to the correct number of significant figures?
questions.explanation: Multiplying the two figures gives 8.5 m exactly, and the two significant figures of the 2.5 s are the weaker precision, so the answer is reported to two figures as 8.5 m. Multiplying or dividing never increases the number of significant figures, since the least precise input caps the whole result, and the trailing zero in 3.40 is itself a counted figure. Adding or subtracting is the opposite rule, governed by the number of decimal places rather than by the number of figures.
questions.hint: Multiply first, then round to the fewer of the two significant-figure counts.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: combine uncertainties when subtracting two measured lengths
questions.stem: A bench length is measured as 12.34 m with an uncertainty of 0.02 m and a shelf length as 7.65 m with the same uncertainty. What is the difference in m?
questions.explanation: The difference is 12.34 - 7.65 = 4.69 m, and its uncertainty is the sum of the two, so the result should be written as 4.69 plus or minus 0.04 m. Pushing the two measurements to their limits confirms the spread: the bench runs from 12.32 m to 12.36 m and the shelf from 7.63 m to 7.67 m, so the shortest possible difference is 4.65 m and the longest is 4.73 m. The midpoint of that range is the same 4.69 m with a half-width of 0.04 m. Uncertainties add in a subtraction because the two measurements are independent, and an error in either one shifts the answer the same way.
questions.hint: Subtract the central values, then add the two uncertainties.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: convert a pressure from N/cm^2 to pascals
questions.stem: A pressure gauge reads 1.3 N/cm^2. What is the same pressure in Pa?
questions.explanation: A pascal is one newton per square metre, and a square centimetre is 1e-4 m^2, so 1.3 N/cm^2 is 1.3 N spread over 1e-4 m^2, which is 13000 Pa. Counting the squares gives the same result: a metre holds 100 cm along each side, so a square metre holds 100 x 100 cm^2, and one newton per cm^2 is therefore 10000 times one newton per m^2. Both routes agree that the answer is in the thousands, which is the check that the square in the denominator was squared rather than left alone.
questions.hint: One pascal is one newton per square metre, and a square centimetre is a ten-thousandth of a square metre.

questions.learningObjective: estimate a count from a step length over a known distance
questions.stem: A walker with a stride of 0.75 m sets out along a straight path 1.0 km long. How many strides does the walk take, to the nearest whole stride?
questions.explanation: The path is 1000 m long and each stride covers 0.75 m, so the count is 1000 divided by 0.75, which is 1334 strides once rounded up. Rounding down would stop short, because one stride fewer covers 999.75 m and the counted strides cover 1000.5 m, so the round-up is forced by the question of whether the walker actually arrives. Only two significant figures are justified here anyway, since the stride length itself is quoted to two.
questions.hint: Divide the distance in metres by the stride length, then round up.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: reject a kinematic formula because its dimensions are wrong
questions.stem: A student wants the time a dropped object takes to fall a distance d, and writes t = d over v squared, where v is a speed. What is wrong with the expression?

options.text: It has the dimensions of a speed, so a numeric answer is impossible
options.misconception: confuses the dimensions of a time with those of a speed

options.text: It is dimensionally sound, but the speed must be squared not halved
options.misconception: accepts a dimensionally impossible formula and invents a missing factor

options.text: It has the dimensions of a length divided by a speed, not of a time
It has the dimensions of a time squared, which is far too large
options.misconception: misreads the dimensions and invents an extra factor of time

questions.explanation: A newton is not involved here, so the only dimensions available are those of a length and a squared speed, which is L divided by L^2 T^-2, leaving T^2 divided by L. That is an inverse speed, not a time, so the formula can never return seconds however the numbers are entered. Time follows from dividing a distance by a speed, or from the square root of 2d over a, and a dimensional check like this one catches the slip before any numbers are touched.
questions.hint: Write the dimensions of d and of v squared, and see what is left over.

questions.learningObjective: convert a density from g/cm^3 to kg/m^3
questions.stem: A block of material has a density of 1.30 g/cm^3. What is the same density in kg/m^3?
questions.explanation: A gram is a thousandth of a kilogram and a cubic centimetre is a millionth of a cubic metre, so the kilogram factor of 1000 is partly cancelled by the millionth from cubing the centimetre, leaving 1300 kg/m^3. Converting separately confirms it: 1.30 g is 0.0013 kg and 1 cm^3 is 1e-6 m^3, and the ratio of those two is the same figure. A density in the thousands of kg per cubic metre is what a solid material should look like, so the size is right as well as the arithmetic.
questions.hint: The metre factor must be cubed, and it is a factor of a hundred per side.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: state what a velocity is a measure of
questions.stem: A student is asked what a velocity describes. Which statement gives the definition that physics actually uses?

options.text: The rate of change of an object's position with time, in a stated direction
The total distance an object covers each second, ignoring direction
options.misconception: drops the direction and keeps only the scalar rate of travel

options.text: The total distance an object has covered since it first began moving
options.misconception: confuses a rate with a running total that keeps accumulating

options.text: The acceleration of an object averaged over the whole of its journey
options.misconception: confuses a velocity with the change in velocity

questions.explanation: Velocity is the time derivative of the position vector, so it carries both a size and a direction and it depends on where the object is now, not on how it got there. The second option is the definition of speed, which is the same quantity with the direction thrown away. A running total is a distance rather than a rate, and the last option describes a rate of change of velocity, one level higher in the calculus than velocity itself.
questions.hint: Velocity answers how fast the position is changing, and in which direction.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: compute an average velocity when the direction of travel reverses
questions.stem: A student runs 60 m east and then 20 m back west, spending 50 s on the trip in all. Taking east as positive, what is the average velocity in m/s?
questions.explanation: Displacement adds with signs, so the runner ends 40 m east of the start, and dividing that by the 50 s of elapsed time gives 0.8 m/s. The distance travelled is 80 m, which is not what belongs on top, because a velocity is a rate of change of position and the second leg undid part of the first. That is the whole difference between average speed and average velocity: the first divides total distance by total time, the second divides displacement by time.
questions.hint: Add the two legs as signed displacements before dividing by the time.

questions.topic: Velocity as a rate of change
questions.learningObjective: explain why a velocity is a rate of change rather than a position
questions.stem: A cyclist rides at a steady 15 m/s along a straight road. What does the phrase 'rides at 15 m/s' describe about the cyclist?

options.misconception: confuses the velocity itself with its rate of change, an acceleration

options.text: How much of the cyclist's energy per second becomes forward motion
options.misconception: confuses a kinematic description with an energy-flux description

options.text: How fast the cyclist's position changes with time along the road
How far the cyclist has travelled since setting out that morning
options.misconception: confuses a rate with the total distance accumulated so far

The total distance is a position-like quantity that keeps accumulating and says nothing about the rate. The third option describes an acceleration, one derivative further on, and the fourth mixes kinematics with an energy statement, which describes something real but is not what a speed measures.
questions.hint: Ask what changes per second: position, distance, or the speed itself.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a speed from a velocity on a closed path
questions.stem: A car travels 120 m around a circular track in 8.0 s, going once around. What is the relationship between its average speed and its average velocity?

options.text: The average velocity is positive and the average speed is zero
options.misconception: swaps the two, treating a closed path as having no path length

options.text: The average speed is positive and the average velocity is zero
Both are positive because the car really is moving during the lap
options.misconception: ignores that displacement is zero when the path closes

options.text: Both are zero because the car ends where it began its lap
options.misconception: believes a zero displacement makes the distance travelled zero too

questions.explanation: The car covers 120 m in 8.0 s, so its average speed is 15 m/s, but it finishes exactly where it started, so its displacement is zero and its average velocity is zero. Speed is built from total distance and cannot be undone by returning to the start, whereas velocity is built from displacement, which cancels over a closed path. This is why a car on a circular track has a nonzero speed at every instant but a zero average velocity over each lap.
questions.hint: Compare the distance covered with the displacement, which is zero for a full lap.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: find the time needed to stop under a constant deceleration
questions.stem: A car moving at 20 m/s brakes with a steady deceleration of 5.0 m/s^2. How long in seconds does it take to come to rest?
questions.explanation: Under a constant deceleration the speed falls linearly, so the time to lose all 20 m/s at 5.0 m/s^2 each second is 4 s. Integrating the slowdown in small time steps gives the same result, since the speed drops by the same 5.0 m/s in every slice of a second and exactly four of them are needed to bring 20 m/s down to zero, with the last slice ending at rest rather than reversing. The answer must be positive: a deceleration cannot stop a car faster than its speed divided by the deceleration, and a negative time would signal a sign error.
questions.hint: The speed changes by the deceleration in each second, so divide speed by deceleration.

questions.topic: Time of a fall under gravity
questions.learningObjective: find the fall time for a body released from rest
questions.stem: A ball is released from rest and falls 45 m. Taking g = 9.8 m/s^2 and ignoring air resistance, how long in seconds does the fall take?

A finite difference confirms the value without any calculus: the position rises from 0.3601 m to 0.3901 m across the 0.02 s step, and dividing that rise by the step returns 1.5 m/s. questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.learningObjective: combine perpendicular components into a single magnitude
questions.stem: A displacement has a component of 3.0 m along one axis and 4.0 m along a perpendicular axis. What is the magnitude of the displacement in m?
questions.explanation: Perpendicular components are independent, so the magnitude follows from Pythagoras, and the root of 9 plus 16 is 5 m. The tempting additions, 3.0 + 4.0 = 7.0 m and 4.0 - 3.0 = 1.0 m, both measure the wrong thing: one treats the components as collinear and the other as opposite. Simple addition applies only when the two displacements lie along the same line, and the 3-4-5 triangle is exactly why 3, 4 and 5 are used in so many examples.
questions.hint: Perpendicular components combine through Pythagoras, not by adding them.

questions.stem: A displacement of 5.0 m lies exactly along the first of two perpendicular axes. What is its component in m along the second axis?
questions.explanation: A vector's component on an axis is its size multiplied by the cosine of the angle from that axis, and a vector lying along the first axis makes a right angle with the second, so the component there is 5.0 multiplied by the cosine of a quarter turn, which is 0 m. The whole magnitude sits in the first component, 5 m, since that axis is where the displacement actually points. The second component is zero rather than unknown, which is the case that trips people up when an angle is left unstated.
questions.hint: Multiply the magnitude by the cosine of the angle between the vector and the axis.

Taking the end coordinates as the displacement would give a distance of 8.6 m, a different quantity that depends on where the origin happens to sit. The shortcut here is that B is the zero vector, so subtracting it changes nothing and A minus B is simply A, which is the general rule that a zero vector is the identity for both addition and subtraction. The second component works out to 0.80, and together they are the familiar 0.60 and 0.80 pair whose squares add to one, which is the check that the vector really is of unit length. options.text: A steadily rising graph does show motion, and it shows no reversal of direction
A rising graph means the object is accelerating, not merely moving
options.misconception: confuses a constant slope with a growing slope

questions.explanation: A position-time graph that rises steadily has a constant positive slope, which is a constant positive velocity: the object moves forward at a steady speed and never reverses. A graph that rises and then falls would be needed to show a body slowing to a stop and returning, and the turn in the graph is exactly where the velocity passes through zero. The slope of this rising graph does not grow, so there is no acceleration, and nothing in its shape suggests a return to the start.
questions.hint: A constant slope means a constant velocity, so read what the slope says about direction.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_MECHANICS
questions.topic: Effect of a graph's scale on a reading
questions.learningObjective: reason about how changing a graph's scale changes a read-off
questions.stem: Two velocity-time graphs cover the same 5 s interval. One is a triangle peaking at 10 m/s, the other a triangle peaking at 6 m/s. What displacement does each give in m?

options.text: 25 m and 15 m, but only because both graphs end at the same time
options.misconception: gives the right areas but the wrong reason

options.text: 25 m for the 10 m/s peak and 15 m for the 6 m/s peak
50 m and 30 m, since the area doubles for a triangular graph
options.misconception: forgets the one-half factor in the area of a triangle

options.text: 10 m and 6 m, since a graph's height is its own displacement
options.misconception: reports the peak height instead of the area under the graph

questions.explanation: Each area is a triangle of base 5 s, so the displacement is one half of base times peak height, giving 25 m for the taller graph and 15 m for the shorter one, in the ratio of the peaks since the bases match. That the two end at the same time is what makes the comparison clean, but the ratio would hold for any shared interval. A rectangular reading of either graph would double the answer, since a triangle is half the rectangle with the same base and height.
questions.hint: Area of a triangle is one half of base times height, and both share the same base.

questions.topic: What a velocity graph cannot show
questions.learningObjective: identify the limit of what a velocity-time graph reveals
questions.stem: A plotted velocity falls linearly from 10 m/s to zero over 4 s. What does that curve establish about the distance covered?

options.text: The distance is the area under the line, whatever shape the line takes
The distance is 10 m, since that is the height the graph starts at
options.misconception: reports the starting speed as though it were the distance covered

options.text: The distance is 40 m, since height and time may simply be multiplied
options.misconception: multiplies a speed by a time and forgets the line is not flat

options.text: The distance is 4 m, since the time axis carries the length directly
options.misconception: reports the duration as though it were a distance

questions.explanation: The area under a velocity-time graph has units of metres per second times seconds, which is metres, and it measures the distance covered whatever shape the graph takes. The line here falls steadily, so that area is the triangle of base 4 s and height 10 m/s, giving 20 m. Multiplying the height by the time, 10 x 4 = 40 m, ignores that the velocity changes throughout the interval and so gives a rectangle rather than the triangle actually under the curve.
questions.hint: Distance is an area, and only the area carries the right units.
